content: 1. Children who are not confirmed to have Ebola virus infection but are exposed to the breast milk of women with confirmed Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) should be classified as contacts. Breastfeeding should be discontinued, and the child should be provided with a suitable breast milk substitute. The child must be closely monitored for any signs or symptoms of EVD for a period of 21 days. 2. If a breastfeeding woman and her child are both diagnosed with EVD, breastfeeding should be immediately stopped. The mother and child should be separated, and appropriate breast milk substitutes should be provided to the child. 3. A woman who has recovered from EVD and has cleared viremia but wishes to resume breastfeeding should wait until two consecutive breast milk tests for Ebola virus, conducted via RT-PCR and spaced 24 hours apart, return negative results. During this waiting period, the child should be fed with a breast milk substitute. 4. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should be offered vaccination with the prequalified Ervebo (Merck) live-replicating rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine during an active Zaire Ebola virus outbreak in affected areas. This should be done within the context of rigorous research or under a compassionate use protocol. 5. The guidelines for managing pregnant and breastfeeding women in the context of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) were developed following universal principles of sexual and reproductive health and rights. They were created in alignment with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development and involved a multidisciplinary group of international experts. 6. Evidence was gathered through a scoping review that identified key questions related to population, intervention/exposure, comparison, and outcomes (PICO/PECO). Due to the limited quality of evidence from the initial review, additional questions were added to strengthen the evidence base. 7. Key questions addressed included the impact of investigational therapies (e.g., ZMapp, REGN-EB3, Remdesivir, mAb114) on maternal, pregnancy, and neonatal outcomes in pregnant women with acute EVD, as well as the effects of induced abortion on outcomes in this population. 8. The guidelines also explored whether Ebola-specific infection prevention and control (IPC) measures should be maintained during pregnancy among EVD survivors to reduce the risk of household and healthcare-associated transmission. 9. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE process, categorizing evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. Low or very low-quality evidence does not necessarily indicate poor study design but reflects limitations in addressing specific PICO questions. 10. Recommendations were formulated based on evidence quality, the balance of benefits and harms, stakeholder values and preferences, resource use, feasibility, applicability, and implementation considerations. 11. Optimized supportive care, including systematic assessment and reassessment, fluid resuscitation, electrolyte and glucose monitoring, treatment of co-infections, and nutritional support, is strongly recommended for all pregnant women with EVD. 12. Investigational therapies, such as REGN-EB3 or mAb114, may be offered to pregnant women with EVD in the context of rigorous research or under the MEURI protocol. These therapies should be considered based on disease severity and the risk-benefit profile. 13. Intensive critical care, including non-invasive ventilation, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, and renal replacement therapy, may benefit pregnant women with EVD, similar to observations in non-pregnant adults. 14. The WHO plans to monitor emerging data and review the guidelines again in 2024 unless significant new evidence warrants an earlier update. Dissemination and implementation of the guidelines will involve online publication, translations, adaptation tools, and collaboration with national and international partners. 15. Recommendations were classified into categories such as recommended, not recommended, insufficient evidence to recommend, recommended only in specific contexts, and recommended only in the context of rigorous research.
